plants.name: Helianthus annuus
plants.description: A tall annual with a large golden flower head made of many small florets surrounded by bright yellow ray petals. Young flower heads track the sun across the sky, and the plant is widely grown for seeds, oil and ornamental use.
plants.bloomingSeason: Mid-summer to early fall in the Northern Hemisphere
plants.location: Native to North America; cultivated worldwide, especially in the United States, Ukraine, Russia and Argentina
plants.funFact: Young sunflower buds exhibit heliotropism, following the sun from east to west each day, but mature flower heads stop moving and typically face east.

plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: A bulbous perennial that sends up pink-lilac, crocus-like flowers in late summer and early autumn without any leaves present. The leaves appear the following spring and die back by early summer.
plants.location: Meadows and woodland edges in Europe, from the British Isles to central Europe; grown in gardens in temperate zones worldwide
plants.funFact: The plant contains colchicine, a toxic compound used in medicine to treat gout, and by plant breeders to induce chromosome doubling. It is often called 'naked ladies' because the flowers appear without leaves.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.description: A small evergreen tree or large shrub with feathery blue-green foliage that covers itself in fragrant, fluffy golden-yellow flower balls. Its flowering marks the end of winter in Australia.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late winter to early spring (August to October) in the Southern Hemisphere
plants.location: Southeastern Australia, including Victoria, South Australia, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory
plants.funFact: Golden Wattle is Australia's national floral emblem, and National Wattle Day is celebrated on September 1, the first day of spring.

plants.name: Solidago canadensis
plants.description: A tall, clump-forming perennial of meadows and roadsides that produces dense, arching plumes of tiny golden flower heads. It is an important late-season nectar and pollen source for bees, butterflies and other insects.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer to autumn (July to October)
plants.location: Native to North America, from Canada through the eastern and central United States; naturalized in Europe and Asia
plants.funFact: Goldenrod is often wrongly blamed for hay fever, but its pollen is heavy and sticky and insect-carried. Ragweed, which blooms at the same time, is the real culprit.
